jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 6 (whether theology is practical or speculative), cross-referencing Aquinas (ST I q.1 a.4) and Scotus's Prologue.

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e113.summary: States the question and first argument for speculative: the noblest science exists for its own sake (Metaphysics I), and theology is the noblest; practical science exists for the sake of work.
claims: The noblest science is for its own sake, so theology is speculative (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e129.summary: Second argument: faith and theology taken as Scripture are the same habit, and faith is speculative, so theology is speculative.
claims: Faith is a speculative habit, and theology as Scripture is the same habit (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e141.summary: Contrary argument: a science directing to good operation is practical, and theology does so (James 1: 'be doers of the word, not hearers only').
claims: Theology directs to good operation, so it is practical

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e154.summary: Lays out three tasks: from what a science is named speculative or practical; if from the end, whether from the proximate or remote end; and the application to theology.

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e170.summary: First task: the speculative/practical distinction is formally from the end and originally from the subject. Formally, because 'speculative' and 'practical' name speculation and praxis (operation outside the intellect), which are the ends of sciences—every habit is for its operation, as happiness is operation according to the most perfect habit—and a science's operation on its object is either mere knowledge of truth or knowledge directing the making of the object, as in architecture or medicine.
claims: The speculative/practical distinction is formally from the end
Every habit is ordered to its operation as end
A science's operation is either knowing truth (speculation) or directing exterior work (praxis)

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e227.summary: Shows the distinction is radically from the object: if the object cannot be done or made by us and our operation cannot make it otherwise, the science only knows truth; if it is agible or factible by us, the science directs the work. Aristotle in De anima III states both the formal (end) and radical (object: the contingent, actual good) differences.
claims: A science is radically speculative or practical from the nature of its object
Practical sciences concern objects that our operation can make otherwise

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e275.summary: Second task: reports the view that theology is named from its remote end—the speculation of heaven—and so is simply speculative, argued from (1) naming by the principal and most intended end, (2) the wayfarer's inability to reach his end in via, and (3) the supreme end naming the supreme habit, as ruling a kingdom names politics.
claims: Some hold theology is named speculative from its remote end, heavenly contemplation (opinion)

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e323.summary: Rejects that view, first argument: the end that names a science is the operation it elicits or directs, but heavenly beatitude is neither elicited nor directly regulated by our theology; no philosopher uses 'speculative' or 'practical' otherwise.
claims: A science is named by the operation it elicits or directs
Heavenly beatitude is neither elicited nor directed by our theology

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e361.summary: Second argument: no science is named from an end to which it is ordered only remotely or through merit. Otherwise moral virtues, remotely disposing to contemplative happiness, would be speculative, and merit itself even more contemplative. And where an end is reached through merit, its attainment follows merit, not the habit: a meritorious old woman or simpleton is more blessed than a doctor of theology with little merit and can reach beatitude without theology, while a wicked doctor cannot. Theology disposes to vision only through merit; the habit of glory disposes immediately.
claims: A science is not named from an end it reaches only remotely or through merit
Attainment of beatitude follows merit, not theological learning
A meritorious simple person is more blessed than a theologian of little merit

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e426.summary: Third argument: since the only content of heavenly beatitude is the vision of God's essence, calling theology speculative from heavenly speculation would make theology a habit of seeing God by essence—which is false (by the inference from a common term with a single instance to that instance).
claims: If theology were named from heavenly speculation, it would be a habit of the beatific vision, which is false

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e463.summary: Reply to the first argument of that view: habits are named by their proper, not common, ends; speculative and practical habits (moral virtues, natural science, metaphysics) can all be ordered to the same remote end of contemplation of God, so naming from that end would make everything speculative or everything practical.
claims: Habits are named from their proper ends, not common remote ends

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e496.summary: Reply to the second: a wayfarer cannot attain the ultimate end simply, but can attain an end suited to his state, namely enigmatic knowledge of the articles about God as Saviour sufficient to direct to salvation.
claims: A wayfarer attains an end proportioned to his state

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e514.summary: Reply to the third: the supreme habit is the speculative habit of glory, not our theology; and one end cannot properly name diverse habits.
claims: The supreme speculative habit is the habit of glory, not wayfarer theology

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e532.summary: Third task: reports the opinion that theology is neither speculative nor practical but affective, since its principal end is love—'the end of the precept is charity' (1 Tim 1), Augustine's dictum on charity, and charity's superiority over faith in this life (1 Cor 13)—and the affective belongs to the will, not the intellect.
claims: Some hold theology is affective, neither speculative nor practical (opinion)

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e568.summary: Durandus accepts for later discussion that theology may be called affective but denies it is neither speculative nor practical. Generally, by its acts every science attains its object either by mere knowledge of truth or by directing further work, so every science is speculative or practical.
claims: Every science is either speculative or practical

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e601.summary: The same from objects: every science's object either is or is not agible or factible by us, a division by affirmation and negation, so every science is practical or speculative.
claims: The division of objects into agible and non-agible is exhaustive

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e621.summary: Even granting theology is affective, its end is either knowledge of truth about charity (making it speculative) or knowledge of how charity and good affection come about in us (making it practical).
claims: An affective theology would still be speculative or practical depending on its end

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e643.summary: Refutes their reasoning: if the affective belonged only to the will, no science—an intellectual habit—could be affective, contrary to their claim; and moral science aims at our being well-affected in will and sensitive appetite yet is practical, so the affective does not exclude the practical.
claims: The opponents' reasoning would exclude any science from being affective
Moral science is affective yet practical

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e674.summary: Clarifies: speculation is in the intellect, but praxis is in another power; a science is called practical as directing cause of praxis, and similarly could be called affective though affection is in the will, as art is factive though making occurs in external things. So an affective theology must still be speculative or practical.
claims: A science is practical as directive cause of an operation in another power
Calling theology affective does not exclude its being speculative or practical

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e698.summary: Applies the results, treating the first and second senses (the third coinciding with the first): theology as the habit of Scripture is simply practical, because its subject is meritorious work, which is agible by us and can be otherwise through our operation.
claims: Theology as the habit of Scripture is simply practical
Meritorious work, theology's subject, is agible by us

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e734.summary: Answers the objection that a practical science requires us to be the sufficient cause of its object while meritorious work requires charity beyond our power: it suffices that human operation be a necessary concause; moreover one can dispose oneself so that God gives charity, and once given, meritorious action is in one's power.
claims: A practical science requires only that human operation be a necessary concause of its object
One can dispose oneself to receive charity, after which meritorious acting is in one's power

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e778.summary: Second proof: Scripture's operation directs work rather than mere contemplation, as countless passages praise doers and rebuke mere hearers; for every column on purely speculative matters there are more than five hundred leaves on practical ones. Because meritorious work requires charity, Scripture exhorts to charity, and calling it affective in this sense—without denying it is practical—is acceptable; the opponents' authorities are so understood. The subject of theology is meritorious work, and its end is love with respect to meritorious work.
claims: Scripture is overwhelmingly practical in content
Scripture may be called affective without denying it is practical
The end of theology is love with respect to meritorious work
concepts: proportion of practical to speculative content in Scripture

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e837.summary: Theology as the habit defending and declaring the principal articles is simply speculative: its subject, God as Saviour, is not agible by us, and its act consists solely in knowing truth, being directly ordered only to declaring and defending the obscure truth of the articles.
claims: Defensive and declarative theology is simply speculative
Its subject, God as Saviour, is not agible by us

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e874.summary: Reply to the first initial argument: the noblest science, the science of the blessed, is for its own sake and purely speculative. Among wayfarer sciences, defensive theology is speculative; deductive theology is not the noblest by subject or by evident certainty, though nobler than other practical sciences in end and subject, and nobler than all human sciences by the light of revelation—which does not make it speculative.
claims: The science of the blessed is the noblest and purely speculative
Practical theology is not the noblest wayfarer science by subject or certainty
Theology's nobility from the light of revelation does not make it speculative

jsnvu6-d1e144-d1e922.summary: Reply to the second: faith in its full breadth, identical with first-sense theology, is a practical habit, since it exists principally that we may become good (faith without works is idle, James 2). Faith narrowed to the principal articles is speculative, as is the theology defending it; but theology that applies the articles to meritorious work is practical—as navigation applies astronomy's purely speculative truth that a certain constellation brings storms to the practical conclusion not to sail.
claims: Faith in its full breadth is a practical habit
Faith of the principal articles is speculative
Theology applying the articles to meritorious work is practical, as navigation applies astronomical truths

jsnvu6-d1e144.summary: Question 6 asks whether theology is practical or speculative. Durandus holds that sciences are formally distinguished as speculative or practical by their ends—speculation (knowing truth) or praxis (directing operation outside the intellect)—and radically by their objects, according to whether these are agible or factible by us. He rejects the view that theology is speculative from its remote end, heavenly contemplation: sciences are named by the operation they elicit or direct, theology reaches beatitude only through merit (a meritorious old woman surpasses a theologian of little merit), and the view would make theology a habit of the beatific vision. He also rejects the claim that theology is neither speculative nor practical but affective: every science is one or the other, and affectivity does not exclude practicality, as moral science shows. Applying this to the senses of theology: as the habit of Scripture (with which deductive theology coincides), theology is simply practical, its subject being meritorious work, for which human operation is a necessary concause, and its end love; it may be called affective in that sense. As the habit defending and declaring the articles, whose subject is God as Saviour, it is simply speculative. The replies distinguish faith in its full breadth (practical) from faith of the articles (speculative), using the analogy of navigation applying astronomy.
claims: Sciences are formally speculative or practical by their ends and radically by their objects
Theology is not named speculative from its remote end in heavenly contemplation
Every science is either speculative or practical; being affective does not exclude being practical
Theology as the habit of Scripture is simply practical, with meritorious work as subject and love as end
Theology as the defense and declaration of the articles is simply speculative
Faith in its full breadth is practical, faith of the articles speculative
